vignette:
She is 66, divorced, and has spent most of her adult life building educational materials for other people’s children, but the memories that shape her now belong to a much older version of herself. She grew up in Oceania and, in her late teens, found herself near combat in a way that would alter the course of her life. She does not describe herself as someone who sought danger; she speaks instead of being caught in it, of learning too early what it means to listen for sudden changes in the air, to read the faces of adults before they speak, and to understand that ordinary sounds can become warnings.

At the time, she was still young enough to believe that fear was something one could recover from with enough sleep and determination. She remembers dust, heat, the sharp metallic smell that seemed to settle into clothing, and the constant background tension of waiting. There were moments when she did not know whether the next noise would be harmless or catastrophic. In later years, she comes back most often to the sensory details: the crack of gunfire in the distance, the weight of her own breath, the way her body would go rigid before her mind could catch up. She learned to move quickly, to keep her head down, to avoid drawing attention. Those habits helped her survive, and they remained in her body long after the danger had passed.

After the combat environment ended, she did not return to the person she had been before. She married, had a family, and eventually divorced, but even in safer years she carried herself as though catastrophe could still arrive without warning. She became a curriculum designer, a role that fit her careful mind and her instinct to organize chaos into something coherent. She is skilled at creating order, structuring lessons, anticipating what others need before they ask. Colleagues have often described her as meticulous and dependable. What they do not always see is the amount of effort it takes for her to remain composed through meetings, deadlines, and unexpected disruptions. She likes work that has sequence and logic because it gives her a sense of control she never quite feels in her body.

For many years, she kept the combat memories mostly sealed away. She rarely spoke about them, even with people close to her. She told herself that what mattered was functioning, and she did function: she raised children, worked steadily, paid bills, and made a life that looked orderly from the outside. But the memories did not remain quiet. They surfaced in fragments—at night, in dreams that left her sweaty and disoriented, or in waking moments when a sound or smell suddenly took her back. A car backfiring can still make her heart lurch before she has time to think. The slam of a door, shouting in the street, helicopters overhead, or news footage of conflict can send her body into a state of alertness that feels immediate and absolute. She becomes tense, watches exits, and has to remind herself that she is here, not there.

Sleep is often broken. She falls asleep with the television on, not because she enjoys it but because silence gives the memories too much room. Even then, she wakes easily. Some mornings she opens her eyes already bracing for something bad. On harder days, she feels irritable and withdrawn, not because she wants to push people away, but because she is tired of being startled, tired of the energy it takes to stay regulated. She notices that she is more comfortable alone than she used to be. Divorce has left her with an ache that is not entirely about the marriage ending; there is also a sense that being fully known might mean being seen in her most vulnerable states, which she has spent a lifetime trying to hide.

She still works, but she no longer has the same ease with change that she once had. A sudden shift in project plans can leave her feeling disproportionately on edge. She rehearses conversations in advance, keeps lists, and prefers routines that help her feel prepared. When she is stressed, she becomes hypervigilant in small ways—checking locks, scanning rooms, sitting with her back to walls. She is aware that others may interpret this as simple fussiness or aging, but she knows it comes from a deeper place. Her body remains convinced that vigilance is necessary.

In recent sessions, she speaks with more sadness than panic. She is beginning to name the grief that has lived beside the fear for decades: grief for the younger self who had to adapt so quickly, grief for years lost to vigilance, grief for the ways her nervous system still behaves as if the conflict has not ended. Yet even as she describes these losses, she also shows the persistence that has defined her life. She keeps showing up to work, keeps revising, keeps building structure from fragments, still trying to make something useful and humane out of what she has carried for so long.
